To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) DXA, geometries, and mechanical testing can be performed on rat femora with a high precision; (ii) the DXA-based bone strength-estimates correlate strongly with the actual biomechanics of the given sites, and (iii) DXA-based bone-strength estimates are not accurate enough in predicting the actual biomechanic characteristics of individual bones.

the DXA measurements are highly reproducible, and the DXA-derived estimates of bone strength correlate highly with the actual mechanical characteristics, but the prediction errors remain relatively large.

(i) DXA is a good tool in the group-level studies of the bone mineral content, density, and geometry of rat femora and the breaking load of the rat femural shaft; (ii) DXA is an acceptable tool for predicting the breaking load of rat femoral neck, but it is a poor tool for predicting the flexural rigidity of the rat femurs.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and testing of the predictive ability of a DXA-based model for the breaking load of rat femora, which is based on the BMD and BMC measurements of rat femoral shafts, necks, and total femoral bones.
the use of DXA in predicting the mechanical characteristics of rat bones.
the development of a new technique for estimating the mechanical characteristics of rat bones in vivo, which would be based on the dual-energy X-ray absorptive properties of the bone.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the DXA-based bone strength-estimative equations should be considered only as a rough approximation of the actual bone strength.
the DXA-based prediction of bone strength is feasible and accurate enough for the group-level analyses, but not for the individual-level analyses.

DXA-based bone mineral variables are good predictors of group-level biomechanical characteristics in rats, but they are not accurate in predicting the biomechanical characteristics at the individual bone level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the case of rat femora, DXA can be used as a tool to study the effects of experimental manipulations on bone strength, but it cannot be used to predict accurately the breaking loads or flexural rigidity of individual rat femora.
DXA is a good method in predicting the group-level biomechanical properties of rat femora.
DXA, geometrics, and biomechanics are all useful methods for the assessment of rat femora.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prediction of bone strength from DXA measurements is not a straightforward process.
DXA-based bone strength-estimation is not a substitute for biomechanical tests.
the prediction of the biomechanics of rat femora using DXA is not a straightforward process.
